articles.title: ENERGY AND DEVOTION IN ELEVENTH-HOUR WORKMEN
articles.author: A. B. Parker
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Brooklyn, N.Y.

paragraphs.text: The brethren will remember that when the materials for the tabernacle had been wrought upon and the work was completed, Moses set up the tabernacle, and as he set it up each part functioned (Exodus 40). He burned the incense on the golden altar for instance, he put the lampstand in the holy place and lighted the lamps, he set the shewbread in order on the pure table; each part functioned as it was set up. I use that as a typical indication that when we come together we should be prepared to function. In principle, the tabernacle is set up locally when we come together. Materials have been prepared and we come together for a purpose.
Not only should we be in faith but we should be prepared to function. Really, there should be no undue waiting in a prophetic meeting—the tabernacle functions when it is set up.

Jehovah had brought in devastating plagues upon Egypt to deliver His people, and He is ready to help us now to be delivered from the world; He is not destroying the world at the moment. He is overthrowing it in the hearts of the saints so that it no longer has its appeal and attraction to the believer. Our thoughts and desires should be related to another world and our outlook should be to make progress in the things of God. We see that when Israel was brought out of Egypt they went through the Red Sea, came into the wilderness,

entered into covenant with God, but immediately broke that covenant, and while Moses was on the mount they turned to idolatry. But the tabernacle was the remarkable product of a heave-offering from a recovered people. The camp had become idolatrous and God came in in discipline and severe judgment. We can trace all this history in our own experience in recent years. We have had part in error and misrepresentation of the truth. Very severe discipline has come upon us, but some of us have been salvaged out of it and I trust we are truly a recovered people. The recovered people brought in abundance the heave-offerings of materials required to construct the tabernacle, to provide a place where God could complacently dwell amongst His people. There was such abundance that Moses had to tell the people not to bring any more. Such feelings are proper to a recovered people. We have had those feelings, dear brethren, but we do not want to cease having them. Let us see that one reason why such departure was allowed was that, as recovered, we would have such depth of feelings that we would bring more than is necessary to furnish God’s dwelling place.

We should not be getting to as few meetings as we feel we can justify, but getting to every meeting. It is thus that we are available all the time for the full service and function of the place where God delights to dwell. Let us therefore learn to function as soon as the tabernacle is set up. Let us be together in exercise about the occasion, acting in faith, on good terms with the blessed Spirit. If so, nothing will be bogging us down, our spirits will not be under burden, our consciences will be free because, as moving in the Spirit, we become a living, operating organism in which the Spirit of God finds delight and to which He delights to add His part.
In the passage I have read reference is made

to early morn, the third hour, the sixth hour, the ninth hour, and the eleventh hour. After the eleventh hour there are no more idle standing in the market-place. The idle ones have been called into activity. John says, “It is the last hour”, 1 John 2: 18. That is the twelfth hour. We have passed the eleventh hour. The Lord expects us all to be at work in the twelfth hour.
Those who came in at early morn did so on the basis of contract; we do not want to do that.

We should come in, dear brethren, conscious of having been shown mercy and compassion which saved us from the errors which we were supporting and condoning. God has saved us in order that we might yet be a peculiar people unto Himself, capable of spontaneous outburst and outflow from our heart’s because of the mercy that has salvaged us and brought us into the vineyard at the eleventh hour. These workmen do not seek a contract, it is wondrous mercy that hired us at all, when it seemed that we would not be hired. But having been hired, let us be “abounding always in the work of the Lord”, knowing that our toil will not be in vain in the Lord (1 Corinthians 15: 58). We are assured that the Lord will do what is right; we have made a miserable failure of things, but He would just say to us, ‘Just trust Me; I will do what is right’. “Will not the Judge of all the earth do right?”, Genesis 18: 25. He certainly will. Dear brethren, we have so much for which to be thankful; we have been shown such mercy that we should not regard as hardship the matter of coming together; we should not be too concerned about the weather; we should be so full of gratitude to the God who has salvaged us out of chaos and has brought us into the clear shining of His presence, that we are ready workers, we are ready to work hard and diligently in the vineyard. There will not be long pauses this evening, and we are going to have a full time. Dear brethren, my purpose in speaking thus
is to stimulate our hearts that we may function acceptably and in a living way in the sphere which the living God has chosen for His dwelling place.

Luke 2: 25–The tabernacle as composed of ten four-coloured curtains with cherubim of artistic work and extending over the ark and other precious pieces of sacred furniture typified, as we know, the saints holding Christ and what is His in their affections. Now this is what we find beautifully exemplified in Simeon, that remarkable man, in the second chapter of Luke, taking up the holy Child into his loving arms and praising God. The four features of his character as mentioned there correspond precisely with the four colours of the tabernacle curtains in Exodus 26: 1, even as to the order in which they are put.

He is said to have been “just”, corresponding with the white twined byssus, and “pious”—that would be the blue, the heavenly colour; he was “awaiting the consolation of Israel”, corresponding to the “kingdom and patience in Jesus” (Revelation 1: 9) of which the purple is expressive; and, finally, the scarlet would find its counterpart in that “the Holy Spirit was upon him”, suggesting the true greatness and glory of man as owned manifestly by God in giving His Spirit. Moreover, he showed forth distinct traits that characterise the cherubim, being submissive to the Spirit’s direction (Ezekiel 1: 12; 10: 20) and marked by a holy discernment in the things of God as to “the Lord’s Christ”, the blessed centre of God’s all-embracing government, who filled his thoughts and outlook. Thus Simeon would represent the features which in our day constitute material for the assembly—and, indeed, he was characteristically “a man in Jerusalem”. May these wonderful features be more richly exhibited in us all!

Luke 19: 11–13; 1 Corinthians 11: 23–26; Revelation 2: 24, These scriptures, you will have noticed, are in the setting of ‘till I come’. It does not say when it will be, but ‘till I come’ or, as Mr. Darby has rendered it in the first scripture, “while I am coming”. It almost looks, dear brethren, as though the Lord Jesus is on the way—“Trade while I am coming”. While He was away and not yet come they were to trade. What a governing matter, what a clock, so to speak, to govern our movements by, “while I am coming”! We are to trade; the Lord is absent, and He is rejected in His absence, as this scripture shows, but we are to trade.

That means you will have to seek out persons with whom you can trade; I would say quite simply that you cannot trade on your own. You can see from a scripture like this the abnormality of a believer choosing to be on his own. In God’s ways, of course, John the apostle was on his own and yet

he addresses the saints as “your brother”; physically on his own but not morally; he is linked with the brotherhood, “I John, your brother and fellow-partaker”, Revelation 1: 9. He was not one who elected to stay at home as, alas, some of our beloved brethren do. How could I trade if I had no one to trade with? You see the abnormality and error of a person isolating himself; he cannot trade, he has no one to trade with, no one with whom to exchange his impressions.

He may still have what he has received, a mina or whatever it was; he has had something given to him. But he never meets anyone, and there it remains in his pocket; he is waiting for the Lord to come but he has perhaps been so shattered by events (I would not speak unfeelingly) that he is not trading. One would long that in the private reading of the Scriptures by such persons the word may become meaningful to them.

“Trade while I am coming”—the Lord is coming. He has given us something; He has given everyone something; you have some impression of Christ that is valuable, in fact I would go as far as to say you have your own distinct and unique impression of Christ. Some feature of His glory, some feature of His Person, has especially laid hold of your soul and it is enshrined there; you are to trade with it, you are to know what it is to exchange it. One wonderful thing that has been said about trading is that it works like this—you have an impression of Christ, and I have an impression of Christ; that is, you have one and I have one; but you share yours with me, and now you have still retained your impression of Christ. By trading with it you did not lose it, you shared it with me; so now you have one and I have two. Then I trade my impression, I share my impression with you; now I possess two, and you possess two. So from one each we have got

two each; that is quite good interest! We should do this, dear brethren, whatever our age, with the brethren we most commonly speak to, gather with, and spend our free time with; we should learn what it is to trade our impressions—‘till I come’. The Lord wants to receive something on His return. He has given you something; is He not worthy of the profit? Is He not worthy of the increase?—“Trade while I am coming”.

I can remember a time when one never did this, never spoke about Christ to others of my generation. Whatever your generation is, whatever the ages of those you meet with, you trade with what you have got; you start it, you start this trading process. When you are with someone you know, you perhaps talk about many things, but try and work in a bit of trading; maybe you will not sustain it for long, we all feel very limited in it, but ask him, that friend of yours, whether he read that piece in the monthly book. Why not in your conversation find time to fit in some thing of this sort, it may not be much, about the Lord’s things, perhaps about somebody’s gospel you still remember? There are gospels that still hang in your mind, you know; you do not have to pretend that you are very spiritual, just be simple about it; ‘I heard him preach once and I can still remember it; he spoke about the glory of Christ’; or,

‘He spoke about faith and how near it was for me to grasp; he helped me over that, he helped me over the matter of faith’. You do not know, but that may become a valuable commodity to that person you have traded with.

Well, the Lord puts it on us all. It does not say what the ages of these bondmen were; I suppose they would cover a wide range of ages, but he asked them to trade and he gave them all something. Now it is obligatory on us, dear brethren, to trade with
what we have. Some have gift; some persons, alas, are not using their gift; there are believers who have gift and they are isolating themselves; it should be a very solemn exercise to them.

Let us all take it to ourselves as to what we have. After all, the Lord gave it to us; it is not our own. There it is, that mina, it is given to you. You look at it sometimes; you may polish it; it is still only a mina; you might rub it, get the ‘Brasso’ out and make it look bright, but it has not gained in value by polishing; you want to trade with it; use it, and get an additional one back. You will find that instead of one mina you have two in your pocket, and then you will have two to trade with, that is, two impressions to share; and you trade again and you finish up with four. Young persons know about arithmetical progressions and geometrical progressions, in some of which a thing is added to while in others they multiply. Well, that is how things develop in christianity, and you can see how persons become enriched by trading.

Some of the nations developed by trading; companies such as the Hudson Bay Company and the East India Company were set up and they traded things abroad and brought things back, rich things, valuable things, rare things. There is such a thing as that spiritually. You see the whole process will cease one day, when you will have made your final transaction. You will have done that final trading, so to speak, and you will be able to present the result to the Lord.

What will it be? What sort of increase will it be? Well, there are many trading persons here, persons you can trade with. Show them something of value and they will trade back something of value. I think the Lord would encourage us to do this, and it is ‘till I come’—
“while I am coming”.

Now in Corinthians we have the Supper. Everyone would know about that, and in the setting here “ye announce the death of the Lord, until he come”. I say again, I trust with a certain amount of feeling, there are some who are not doing this, they are not announcing the death of the Lord until He come. Let our prayer be, dear brethren, that the Lord may in His sovereignty work with such to gather them in to answer to Him. Paul received it from the Lord; it is really obligatory on us to take the Supper as soon as we are able to. If we have love for the Lord, and desire for it, and are able to appreciate at least something of what the Supper involves, we are to do it—“ye announce the death of the Lord, until he come”.

Maybe some young one here is exercised about it. There is some stirring, some desire in relation to it; you have love for Christ; you realise He died for you and shed His blood. You understand when you look at the emblems on the table on the Lord’s day that the loaf represents His body in which He did God’s will, a body that was wholly devoted to God’s will. You realise that the cup speaks of His blood, the blood that was shed for many for remission of sins. You by faith have accepted that it was shed for you. There is, week by week, some stirring in your heart to do what He requested you to do. Do not let the exercise drop. If you have any feeling that way, any stirring, any desire, learn to ask yourself why you want to do it—not just because your friend does it, or someone older, or maybe someone younger; that is not a sound enough basis; but if you want to do it out of love for the Lord Jesus, and if you have some appreciation, some understanding, of what it involves, I do not think you will find the brethren will make it difficult. You do not have to be a particular age.
At school the authorities

have arbitrarily drawn a line at certain stages in your life, at eleven years, for instance, but God has not done that; you do not have to be a certain age, and yet you need to understand something of what you are going to do. ‘Till I come’; it will not be for always, you see, and the Lord will come soon. We announce the death of the Lord till He come.

Now I would like to refer to Revelation. The saints are here envisaged in this aspect of the church, Thyatira. We sometimes speak of this historically; it represents Romanism; Sardis represents Protestantism; both are around us, and there are some in both whom the Lord notices. It is a great comfort, dear brethren, that the Lord notices persons; you say, ‘Even in Rome?’, yes, even in Rome. To “the rest” He says, “to you I say”, as if the Lord is addressing them in the midst of a profession that has become so political, claims so much, and in fact in many ways has come so near the truth, and yet has handled it so badly. The Lord looks right through the whole fabric, the whole of the system with all its appurtenances and all that is around it, and He addresses you, “To you I say, the rest who are in Thyatira”.
Now we can bring it forward to ourselves. The Lord searches out in any circumstance, or any failure of the church; His eyes see, the Lord sees, dear brethren, and His judgment is absolute.
His inclement is unerring. His judgment is exact; what precision is in the Lord’s judgment!

We may have a general judgment that may be right, but we may over-err in one direction; the Lord’s judgment is precise. “To you I say, the rest ... I do not cast upon you any other burden”. What grace, dear brethren! ‘I know the problems you have got; I know you find it difficult; everyone else goes to
church or chapel, you go to a little meeting room, maybe into somebody’s house; persons ask you where you go and you have to say it is to So-and-so’s house’. It is a burden, is it not?

You would fain go to a more impressive building, I am speaking to young ones especially. It is a burden, the Lord will not add to your burden. He says, “To you I say … I do not cast upon you any other burden; but what ye have hold fast till I shall come”. So what have I? We were encouraged at one time actually to write down what we have. It is not a bad idea; many spiritual men have kept notebooks in which they wrote down thoughts on certain scriptures, or certain impressions.

Now supposing we were given a pencil and paper and wrote down what we had. You say, ‘I have the forgiveness of sins; I have the Spirit’. Can you write that down? Would you say, ‘I think I have the Spirit’? Well, I was once in a stage like that; no one is going to be cross because that is as far as you write; but you write it down, let the thing become crystalized in your soul. It often helps to ask oneself questions as to where am I, and what have I that I am sure of? I think, the Lord would develop us in this, in integrity, so that we speak not in terms but as knowing the possession of a thing. What you have, the Lord says, hold fast.

What have you, dear brethren? What have I? I may say, in a general sense, I have the truth; well, what truth? It is too general; if you had the truth, then you could write it all down. Do you think you could? I do not think I could write all the truth down. Of course, we know what we mean when we say, ‘He has got the truth’—the general bearing of the truth, the general outline of the truth. Paul laid that on Timothy; he said, Have an outline of it; not a compendium of it, an

encyclopaedia in thirty-odd volumes, but an outline of it, a notebook of it. Get a notebook and write down what you have; fill it up with what you have in the way of the knowledge of God, what you are sure about; not what you think you should have, but what you have; be real, learn to develop integrity in yourself, so that you do not assume to know more than you have. We have all failed in this, dear brethren, probably none more than I, but the Lord is very tender; even in relation to that He is very tender; He does not cut you off because you say something more than your measure and more than you know, you perhaps use some borrowed expression.

You remember that man in 2 Kings 6 who borrowed an axe and as he was felling a beam the head of the axe fell off; it was not his, you see. It went in the water and he said, “Alas ... and it was borrowed!” A very humbling experience, is it not? ‘Well, I thought I had it, but now I find I have not got it, it has gone; it is down there somewhere’. The Lord is very tender; the man of God said, “Where did it fall?” He cast in a stick and made the iron to swim. And he said, “Take it up to thee”. Get it, make sure; “Lay hold of eternal life”, the apostle says to Timothy. Do not be nebulous about it, be concrete, learn integrity. We all feel very shallow; we all use borrowed expressions, but the Lord is very gracious to us. “What ye have”, the Lord says, “hold fast till I shall come”.

Well, you say, what have I got? The Lord has left certain things; He has left certain impressions; generally the truth is known amongst us, thank God; we have had an outline; there is such a large amount of ministry that the teaching is known; what we have is extremely valuable, but let us make sure that we have it, not only in terms, but that we have got it, so that we actually express the thing. You

talk about the new covenant, God shining, and Moses coming down with his face shining, but you come into the meeting and display it, the new covenant, or reconciliation. If you have it, you will display it; the truth shines out in persons. Mr. Taylor said it is greater to represent God than to minister the truth. It is greater to be able to represent a thing than to speak about it. What you have, the Lord says, hold fast till I come. Well, there is a good deal that has been granted in the area of the recovery; in the midst of christendom there is an area in which God worked; it was for the whole of christendom, but not everybody took advantage of it, but many did, thank God, and the continuation of that is still to be found. What you have, what I have, dear brethren, let us hold fast. You see, it is for us to maintain it and to pass on to the generation to follow, but let us hold it in integrity and reality, not only in terms but in the vitality of it.

So Paul says to Timothy, “Be not therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner; but suffer evil along with the glad tidings”, 2 Timothy 1: 8. Mr. Darby’s note on that verse speaks as to the ‘personification of the gospel’. Paul might have said, ‘Suffer evil along with me’, but he says, “Suffer evil along with the glad tidings”; there was a personification of the glad tidings in Paul. In fact, he indicates to the Corinthians that his gospel was so clear that if it was veiled it was veiled in those that were lost, in the unbelieving. So “What ye have hold fast till I shall come”. Well, may we, dear brethren, be helped to do it; it is just while He is coming, you see. Will the Lord find the real thing, or will He find merely the doctrine, the letter? The Pharisees and the scribes often had the letter. The Lord asked the young man about the neighbour and he could

quote, but did he have the real thing? Have I the real thing? When the Lord comes He will look for the real thing. Someone will have it, some souls will have it, both old and young, the real thing. Well, let us be real, dear brethren; therefore may the Lord help us—it is just while He is coming, ‘till I come’—for His name’s sake.

articles.title: THE GREATEST THINGS FOUND IN LIMITATION
articles.author: L. A. Barlow

paragraphs.text: A wonderful thing about the Scriptures is that in them God has provided for our day, a day that is outwardly marked by small things. The question is raised, “Who hath despised the day of small things?”, Zechariah 4: 10. I think God would encourage us by showing us that what is vital is often outwardly small. We may well desire numbers, and surely God will have His numbers, as Revelation shows, but I believe that what God is looking for at present is persons of substance. When Ezra arranged for the bringing up of the vessels for the house of God, the great question was the weight, rather than the number (see Ezra 8). Once God has what He wants, He can always add to it, as He did at the beginning. In Jerusalem at the commencement of this dispensation reference is made in the Acts to the number of the names, showing that each person was of special value. I believe that God is looking for a similar answer now we are at the end. You will recall the two vessels of shining copper, precious as gold, that
were brought back from Babylon (Ezra 8: 27); that is what God is seeking in our day. May we therefore be encouraged and concerned to consider what is of substantial value, rather than just numbers.

It is this that made me refer to the scripture in Luke’s gospel. The greatest thing that had ever happened in this world had occurred, a wonderful thing!—the Saviour, who is Christ the Lord, had been born, the glorious Person who will fill a universe for God; and yet how limited was the number of persons who were aware of it. A lowly Babe in Bethlehem’s manger, was said to be the sign. I think it is a sign for our day, that the greatest things are to be found in conditions of outward smallness and weakness. There was nothing outwardly attractive by way of what is natural, but all was connected with the greatest things possible, and indicated wondrous expansion, “a babe wrapped in swaddling-clothes, and lying in a manger”. Think of it; a Babe, outwardly helpless, yet the glorious Person who is going to fill the universe. Oh may we be encouraged and not despise the day of small things, seeing that it is part of the ways of God that His things are, generally speaking, marked by outward smallness in this world, but connected with what heaven itself can take account of, “a multitude of the heavenly host”, as it says here. May we get heaven’s view of things. This lowly Babe involving “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good pleasure in men”.

I think this helps us, beloved, to accept what may appear to be outwardly small, but should nevertheless make us concerned that things are valuable and real. I believe there is a need to relate divine operations to the position in which we may find ourselves at the present time.
Men may talk of things dying out, but the very existence of things
in outward smallness is of immense encouragement, for it is so often connected with God’s direct movements. What a circle of things surrounded the birth of this glorious Person.

Another has referred to it as a sterile area of things where there was the exclusion of what was incompatible. May we find grace to secure and maintain the conditions that were found with these persons in Luke. It is very interesting what is mentioned in these chapters, the Lord Himself as a Babe, and then as a Boy. His father and mother, I suppose, relatively young. Then there is Simeon, an older man, and Anna, an older woman, varying generations but all connected with what God was doing. I think this would be an encouragement to us, no matter what age we are, and cause desire with us that we might be content with what may appear small and is despised but is nevertheless connected with the revelation of the greatest things. Luke was with Paul at the end, showing, I believe, that it is in such an area as is portrayed in the beginning of his gospel that the greatest thoughts of God are treasured, valued, and protected now. May we be amongst those who are characteristically engaged in doing such things at the present time.
The scripture in Judges also relates to a time of great restriction. The Midianites were attempting to cut off the food supply. It is interesting to trace the references to the Midianites.

It was they who took Joseph out of the pit and sold him. May we be preserved from using christianity for our own personal advantage! It is a sobering thing that many have used it in that way, turning christianity into a means of personal present gain. Such fleshly features tend to cut off believers from the true food supply. The same nation again appears (Numbers 22) as the people of God are about to enter the land. The Spirit having been given, in type, there

was a forward movement. We then have Balaam’s parable, viewing the saints in relation to the great thoughts of God, and the Midianites come forward with an attempt to corrupt the people of God, to hinder them from entering the land. They refer to what is of nature, beloved, which would tend to divert the saints from entering into their true heavenly portion.

In Numbers 25 those involved in corruption were persons of influence. Scripture actually mentions the name of a prince of Israel. How many have been diverted by having prominent persons before them! There is a great need to have before us what all the saints are according to the thoughts of God.

To revert to the scripture read, we find Gideon threshing wheat in a wine-press, in conditions, you might say, which are abnormal and restricted. But, typically, he values the saints according to what they are as related to Christ. It is interesting that when the Greeks come up in John 12, as if to make something of the Lord publicly. He immediately refers to the grain of wheat falling into the ground and dying in view of bringing forth much fruit. May we be in constant exercise to bring in the needed food which will help the saints to understand their blessed relationship with that glorious Man who is out of death. I suppose the wine press would refer to the pressures which may come in as we accept the limitations, but it would also, no doubt, have an allusion to something being produced for God. It is a great thing to help the saints increasingly to know what they are as related to the purposes of God and the glorious place that He has in His mind for them, because it is in the enjoyment of these heavenly things that the service of God is carried on in a vital way.
As we know, the actual experience later on of

the men who were with Gideon involved constant reduction, but as a result the whole issue in relation to Midian was met and conditions of peace established for all Israel. I believe, beloved, that God will add, but He will add where there is what can be added to. Any shining out always involves earthen vessels being broken. Paul refers to “Bearing about in the body the dying of Jesus, that the life also of Jesus may be manifested in our body”, 2 Corinthians 4: 10. May we be simply concerned, in spite of all the difficulties, to provide food in season. It is possible, beloved. Maybe the conditions do not appear ideal; they were certainly not ideal for Gideon, but nevertheless he is carrying on this service. No matter what the world might think of it, an angel of Jehovah appeared to him and said, “Jehovah is with thee, thou mighty man of valour”. It is a great thing to have some sense that God is with us in relation to what we are doing and can recognise us in this way. May we value heaven’s commendation rather than the approbation of men. How good if we qualify for those beautiful words of the Lord Jesus, “Well, good and faithful bondman … enter thou into the joy of thy lord”, Matthew 25: 23. It is open to any one of us to qualify, but be assured the Lord will only say that to us if it is really true of us. May this scripture encourage us, in spite of the outward conditions, to continue to be concerned to provide food.

In the scripture in John’s gospel it is again a question of a few persons. As others have noted, as you proceed in John’s gospel, during the Lord’s life here numbers tended to become reduced. In the end you have one woman at the tomb. What a woman! She had but one object, that glorious Person. She represents what is of the assembly vitally. May we be concerned that in our localities
there is something that answers to the assembly in this way. These two chapters—John 11

and 12 are peculiarly attractive for they speak of the love of that glorious Person for individuals, for you and for me, but His great objective is to set us together in relation to Himself. Sometimes gatherings are mainly composed of persons who have natural relationships with one another. No doubt this is of God, because He loves the idea of a family. When the question of nations will cease, God will have a universe that is composed of families, every family named of the Father, but the great thing is that our vital relations together should be connected with our links with Christ. The Lord had to come into the circumstances of those He loved in order that He might be the true centre, that they might understand that what was lasting and abiding was their link with Him and their links with one another through Him. It is a great thing when we too come to that, that He is the resurrection.

Delightful as natural relationships are, they are subject to death. But God has given us links that are beyond the range and power of death. They are links with this glorious Person who is the resurrection and the life.
So the chapter read shows persons who are set together with one objective—to provide for Him, each one serving in his or her own place. There are no complaints from Martha.

Sometimes we complain about one another as occupied with the natural sphere of things, but it is a wonderful thing when we understand our links with one another as associated with the Son of God. If He loves each one of us here, surely it should be simple for us to love one another. And the effect of that love, as known by us each one, would be to create a desire to provide collectively for Him and Him alone. As He becomes, where He is, the centre for each one of us personally, we are set together in a wondrous way

that nothing can possibly interfere with. The result of that is that something is available, not necessarily very large, but of tremendous value, capable, indeed—as it was here when released in relation to the One who was filling the affections of His own—of filling the house with the odour of the ointment. What that must have meant to the Lord Jesus!

All this occurred in the presence of Judas, the betrayer, and with the Lord’s actual death lying just ahead of Him. Of course, what lies ahead of Him now is the day of His glory, when everything will be subject to Him and ministering to His pleasure. What a privilege that in the day in which we find ourselves we can provide Him with something which gratifies His own heart. Mary did this in view of the day of His burial. We have the privilege of doing things in anticipation of the day of the manifestation of His glory. May God just help us and encourage us to see what is available to us in the day in which we find ourselves—a day of small things outwardly, but, as Malachi reminds us, a day in which God finds that which is pleasing to Him. Books are written and persons are spared, because of what He finds for His own pleasure in them. May God help us increasingly to see what He is doing so that we may not despise the day of small things, but may fill out our, part in providing for the saints and for the praise and service of God.
Pray without ceasing, pray,
God’s throne’s a throne of grace;
His power exceeds the direst needs
Of those who seek His face.
In everything give thanks,
E’en when the heavens seem brass.
The Father’s love is e’er above
Whatever comes to pass.
If one should suffer ill—
His sickness find no balm—
Then let him pray and in this way
His prayer begets a psalm.
But persevere in prayer;
This is our subject part;
Though our request may have to rest
Till God has searched the heart.
In Spirit we must pray,
But ne’er repeat in vain.
The Saviour’s name God’s ear must claim
And thus our cause maintain.
Then prayer will turn to praise,
And praise to worship lead.
God glorified, hearts satisfied
For we can meet His need.

articles.title: THE TESTIMONY TO DIVINE LOVE IN DEATH
articles.author: D. R. Freeman

paragraphs.text: John in his gospel presents what is of God from the divine side, over against all the ruin and darkness of man. Thus we have the witness to men of His love in redemption in the gift of His Son. It was this that the Saviour presented as risen from the dead to His disciples in showing to them His hands and His side (John 20: 20). His hands told plainly where He had been as crucified, made sin and lifted up to die, thus associated with the totality of our ruin and sin. His side as pierced by the soldier but evinced the fullest possible testimony to divine love in the blood and water which flowed, the answer both judicial and moral to man’s guilt and need. So His word in John 20 was, “Peace”. The very fullest expression of divine love is towards us and this could not be gainsaid. What else could the disciples do but rejoice, or we, as we discern the love of God in all its fulness towards us, and, indeed, also for all, commended to us as it is and shed abroad through the service of the Holy Spirit in our hearts?
Kingston, Ont.

paragraphs.speaker: AM
paragraphs.text: I A SINGER? Paul exhorts both the Ephesian and Colossian believers to be singers—
“Singing and chanting with your heart to the Lord”, Ephesians 5: 19.

It is a happy and healthy state of soul—a normal state—that produces singing. Paul was a singer. Amid the midnight darkness of the jail at Philippi there went up to heaven a rich harmony as Paul and Silas “in praying, were praising God with singing”, Acts 16: 25. What music continually goes up to heaven from the saints, in all parts of the earth, and in all kinds of circumstances, as the sound of thankful praise arises from hearts which joy in God and are full of Christ. Circumstances may be very testing, but they are not to rob us of the source of our joy—all that is in God, and in Christ, made real in the Holy Spirit’s power—so that from satisfied hearts goes up a note of thankful praise. May we each be constantly in it!
Heaven forms in a sense part of the world to come, but heaven is not the world to come. The world to come takes in both heaven and earth, “the things in the heavens and the things upon the earth”.

Jonathan acts as a man. In all difficulties the real solution depends on manliness—to act in a manly way. Jonathan had a great place in Israel. Why should he not use any advantage he has? Any advantage we may have we should use in favour of Christ.
